name: Tramadol + Paracetamol
meta: Tramadol Hydrochloride: Centrally acting opioid analgesic; Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): Non-opioid analgesic and antipyretic

Psychotropic substance under the NDPS Act, 1985 and Schedule H/H1 of the Drugs & Cosmetics Rules (brought under NDPS as psychotropic in 2018); Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): Non-prescription for plain low-strength oral forms; Schedule H in combinations
sections: White crystalline powder (hydrochloride), freely soluble in water.
White crystalline powder, odourless with bitter taste; melting point 169 °C; sparingly soluble in water.

Tramadol Hydrochloride: A synthetic codeine analogue; brought under India's NDPS Act as a psychotropic substance in 2018 due to misuse. First approval/introduction: Patented 1972; launched 1977 in West Germany (Grünenthal GmbH); US FDA 1995. Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): On the WHO List of Essential Medicines and the most widely used analgesic–antipyretic worldwide; onset ~37 minutes after an oral dose. First approval/introduction: Synthesised 1877 (Harmon Northrop Morse); clinical use from 1887; widely marketed from 1950s.

Paracetamol has fast onset; tramadol provides longer-lasting analgesia via opioid and monoaminergic mechanisms. Low-dose combination gives synergistic analgesia with fewer adverse effects than higher doses of either.

Tramadol Hydrochloride Weak mu-opioid agonist (mainly via active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol, formed by CYP2D6) plus inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake. Receptor / target profile: Racemate: (+)-enantiomer and M1 are mu-opioid agonists (M1 ~6x more potent); (+)-tramadol inhibits serotonin and (−)-tramadol norepinephrine reuptake.

Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) Inhibits prostaglandin synthesis centrally (COX in CNS), modulates descending serotonergic pathways and acts on the hypothalamic heat-regulating centre; weak peripheral anti-inflammatory action. Receptor / target profile: Central COX inhibition (peroxidase site) and actions of metabolite AM404 on TRPV1 and endocannabinoid systems; weak peripheral anti-inflammatory activity.
Hepatic – CYP2D6 (O-desmethyltramadol, M1, active) and CYP3A4 (N-demethylation); glucuronidation
Summary: Bioavailability ~75%; Tmax ~2 h. Metabolised by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4. Half-life ~6 h (metabolite ~7 h). Renally excreted.
Hepatic – glucuronidation, sulfation; ~5–10% CYP2E1 to NAPQI
Summary: Rapidly absorbed; Tmax 0.5–1 h. Glucuronidated and sulfated; small fraction via CYP2E1 to toxic NAPQI (detoxified by glutathione). Half-life 1–3 h.
Chronic pain – osteoarthritis, low back pain, when NSAIDs are unsuitable
Adults and adolescents ≥12 years: 2 tablets initially, then 1–2 tablets every 4–6 h as needed
Maximum 8 tablets/day (300 mg tramadol, 2.6 g paracetamol)
CrCl <30 mL/min: dosing interval ≥12 h; max 2 tablets every 12 h
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
CrCl <30: dose every 12 h, max 200 mg/day; avoid ER.
Cirrhosis: 50 mg every 12 h; avoid ER.
>75 years: max 300 mg/day; increased seizure and hyponatraemia risk.
Contraindicated <12 years; avoid 12–18 years with respiratory compromise or after tonsillectomy.
Avoid; neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome with prolonged use.
Max 2–3 g/day in chronic liver disease or chronic alcohol use; avoid in severe active disease.
Usually well tolerated; reduce max dose if frail/low weight.
Acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, opioids or psychotropics
Use with or within 14 days of MAO inhibitors
Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease
Addiction, abuse and misuse – controlled drug; dispense limited quantities
Respiratory depression, especially with benzodiazepines/CNS depressants
Seizure risk (dose-related; higher with SSRIs, TCAs)
Withdrawal on abrupt cessation; hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia
Hepatotoxicity with overdose or >4 g/day – avoid duplicate paracetamol-containing products
Caution in chronic alcohol use, malnutrition, G6PD deficiency
SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs, triptans (serotonin syndrome, seizures)
Metoclopramide speeds absorption; cholestyramine reduces it
Tramadol Hydrochloride: With or without food; no alcohol.
Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): With or without food; avoid alcohol.
Tramadol Hydrochloride: Respiratory status; sedation; misuse; sodium; glucose.
Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): LFTs if high doses long-term or risk factors.

Tramadol Hydrochloride: Miosis, vomiting, respiratory depression, seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse. Airway support; naloxone (may not reverse seizures); benzodiazepines for seizures. Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): Potentially fatal hepatic necrosis; early symptoms may be absent. Give N-acetylcysteine as per nomogram – urgent treatment.
Edwards et al., 2002 – pooled dental-pain trials: combination more effective than either component.
Effective in chronic OA and low back pain (Peloso et al., 2004).
Never combine with alcohol, sleeping pills or anxiety medicines
Keep out of reach of children
Do not exceed 4 g/day from all sources
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
